theme: The prologue in heaven; Job’s suffering begins
readingInstruction: Read Job 1:1-2:13. This is the prologue, and it is the only place in the book where you are allowed to see behind the curtain. Read it as a story told in two settings: the courts of heaven and the ash heap on earth. Notice that Job never gets to read these two chapters.
settingTheScene: You have finished the Law and are now entering the wisdom literature. Job is probably the oldest story in this stretch of the Bible. The details point to the age of the patriarchs: Job’s wealth is counted in livestock, he offers sacrifices as the head of his own household, and there is no mention of Israel, the exodus, or the law of Moses. The land of Uz lies outside the covenant people. That matters. God is showing you a man who knows him and fears him before the nations are sorted into Israel and everyone else. The book asks the oldest question people ask: why do the righteous suffer? And it will not let you answer too quickly.
observation: Job is introduced as “blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil” (1:1). The narrator tells you this before anything goes wrong.
Job is wealthy, with seven sons, three daughters, and enormous flocks. He also offers burnt offerings on behalf of his children, “for Job said, It may be that my children have sinned” (1:5).
The scene shifts to heaven, where the sons of God present themselves before the LORD, and Satan comes among them (1:6).
The LORD, not Satan, brings up Job: “Have you considered my servant Job?” (1:8).
Satan’s accusation is that Job fears God only because God pays him for it, “Does Job fear God for no reason?” (1:9).
God sets a limit. Satan may touch what Job has but not Job himself (1:12). In chapter 2, he may touch Job’s body but must spare his life (2:6).
Four messengers arrive one after another, and Job loses oxen, donkeys, sheep, camels, servants, and finally all ten of his children (1:13-19).
Job worships: “The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (1:21). The narrator adds, “In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong” (1:22).
Job’s wife says, “Curse God and die” (2:9). Three friends arrive and sit with him in silence for seven days (2:11-13).
interpretation:
The first thing the prologue does is settle a question that the rest of the book will keep raising. Job’s suffering is not a punishment for sin. The narrator says so, and God says so twice (1:8; 2:3). If you forget this, you will read the next thirty-nine chapters the way Job’s friends do, looking for what Job must have done wrong.

The second thing the prologue does is show you that suffering has a larger setting than the person suffering. Satan appears as an accuser. His charge is a charge against God as much as against Job: that God’s servants love him only because he pays them well, and that if the payment stops, so will the worship. The question on trial is whether God is worth loving for himself. Job does not know he is on trial. He does not know any of this is happening. That is a hard truth and a necessary one: sometimes the most important thing going on in your suffering is something you cannot see.

Notice the limits. Satan is not an equal of God. He cannot act until he receives permission, and the permission has a boundary every time. This is not a comfortable picture, because it means God is sovereign even over the hand that strikes Job. But it is also the only picture in which suffering has a limit and an end. The book will not explain to Job why God permitted it. It will show that God remained in charge.

Then look at Job’s response. He tears his robe and shaves his head, which are the actions of real grief, and then he falls to the ground and worships. He does not pretend that nothing happened. He does not say that it is fine. He says that the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away, and he blesses the name of the LORD anyway. Chapter 2 sharpens the test. His wife, who has lost everything too, tells him to give up. Job answers, “Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?” (2:10). That is not cold stoicism. It is a man who has decided that God is not only a giver of gifts.

The last scene is the quietest. The friends sit with him for seven days and say nothing. It is the best thing they will do in the whole book.
connection: Jesus’ own story echoes Job’s. He too was declared righteous by the Father (“This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased”) and then led into suffering at the hand of the accuser (Matthew 3:17-4:11). Revelation 12:10 names Satan as “the accuser of our brothers.” James holds up Job as an example of steadfastness (James 5:11).
application:
First, if you are suffering now, hear that your suffering is not automatic proof of anything about you. Do not assume that God is angry, and do not assume that he is absent.

Second, remember that Satan has a leash. Nothing in your life, including the worst thing, falls outside the limits God sets.

Third, practice Job’s honesty. You can grieve openly and worship at the same time. Say the true thing about the pain and the true thing about God, and do not let either cancel the other.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that nothing touches your life beyond the limit he sets.
Ask him to keep you from believing he has turned against you when you suffer.
Pray for someone who is grieving today.
